metadata.name: Gout
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - but exclude septic arthritis (emergency) in an acute hot joint
metadata.severity: Painful acute attacks; chronic tophaceous disease and joint damage if untreated

overview.short_description: A crystal arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals due to chronic hyperuricaemia, presenting as acute, severe, self-limiting attacks of a hot, swollen joint (classically the big toe).
overview.detailed_description: Gout is the commonest inflammatory arthritis. Acute attacks are intensely painful monoarthritis, often of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra). It results from long-standing raised serum urate leading to crystal deposition; attacks are triggered by fluctuations in urate. Management is anti-inflammatory treatment of attacks plus long-term urate-lowering therapy (treat-to-target) to prevent recurrence and tophi. The key safety step is excluding septic arthritis in an acute hot joint.
overview.pathophysiology: Sustained hyperuricaemia (overproduction or, more often, renal under-excretion of urate) leads to monosodium urate crystal formation in and around joints; crystals trigger an intense innate inflammatory response (NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1beta).
overview.etiology: Hyperuricaemia from reduced renal excretion (most), increased production (purine-rich diet, alcohol - especially beer, high fructose, cell turnover), or drugs (diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin). Genetic and metabolic-syndrome associations.
overview.natural_history: Recurrent acute attacks over years; without urate lowering, progresses to chronic tophaceous gout with joint damage; associated with cardiovascular and renal disease.
overview.prognosis: Excellent with effective urate-lowering therapy to target; poor adherence leads to recurrent attacks and joint damage.

prevalence.value: Common; affects a few percent of adults, rising with age and metabolic syndrome.

mortality.value: Low directly; associated with increased cardiovascular/renal risk.

epidemiology.age_groups: Middle-aged and older adults; postmenopausal women.
epidemiology.sex_predominance: Much more common in men (women's risk rises after menopause).

risk_factors.lifestyle: Purine-rich diet (red meat, shellfish), sugary/fructose drinks, dehydration.
risk_factors.alcohol: Strong risk factor, especially beer and spirits.
risk_factors.obesity: Strong risk factor (part of metabolic syndrome).
risk_factors.family_history: Common; genetic influences on urate handling.
risk_factors.genetic_factors: Polymorphisms in urate transporters; rare enzyme disorders.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Chronic kidney disease, hypertension, obesity, dyslipidaemia; prior gout.

chief_complaints.complaint: Sudden severe pain, redness and swelling of a joint (often the big toe)
Recurrent attacks in the same/other joints

symptoms.symptom: Acute monoarthritis - rapid-onset severe pain, swelling, redness, warmth

symptoms.importance: Classic site; strongly suggestive when present

symptoms.symptom: Tophi (firm urate deposits, e.g., ear, fingers, Achilles)
Fever/systemic upset with a hot joint
symptoms.importance: Overlaps with septic arthritis - must exclude infection

negative_findings.finding: Joint aspirate with NO organisms/negative culture but negatively birefringent urate crystals
negative_findings.why_important: Confirms gout and excludes septic arthritis (the key differential)

negative_findings.finding: No fever, gradual onset, polyarticular pattern without prior gout
negative_findings.why_important: Makes acute gout less likely; consider other arthritides

history_questions.question: Did the pain come on rapidly (hours) and is it very severe in one joint, especially the big toe?
history_questions.why_ask: Rapid, severe monoarthritis (podagra) is typical of gout

history_questions.question: Have you had similar attacks before, and any tophi?
Any fever or feeling systemically unwell?
Alcohol intake, diet, diuretics/aspirin, kidney disease?
Any cardiovascular/renal disease or metabolic syndrome features?
history_questions.why_ask: Associated comorbidity and drug-safety for urate lowering

physical_examination.expected_finding: Hot, red, swollen, exquisitely tender (often first MTP)

physical_examination.examination: Look for tophi (ears, fingers, elbows, Achilles)
physical_examination.expected_finding: Firm chalky deposits in chronic gout
Usually afebrile; fever raises concern for infection

physical_examination.examination: Assess other joints and cardiovascular/renal status

vital_signs.temperature: Usually normal (low-grade fever can occur; high fever suggests sepsis)

laboratory_tests.test_name: Joint aspiration (synovial fluid) for crystals and culture
laboratory_tests.indication: Definitive diagnosis and to EXCLUDE septic arthritis
laboratory_tests.expected_result: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped MSU crystals; no organisms

laboratory_tests.indication: Support diagnosis and guide urate-lowering therapy (check ~2-4 weeks after an attack settles, as it can be normal/low acutely)
laboratory_tests.expected_result: Usually raised (may be normal during an acute attack)
laboratory_tests.rule_out: A normal level during an attack does not exclude gout

laboratory_tests.indication: Assess inflammation, renal function and comorbidity

imaging.expected_findings: Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges in chronic gout

other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Tophus aspiration/biopsy shows urate crystals if needed
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Synovial fluid culture to exclude septic arthritis

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Definitive diagnosis is demonstration of monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid or a tophus. A confident clinical diagnosis can be made for a typical acute podagra with hyperuricaemia and prior similar attacks; the ACR/EULAR classification criteria can support diagnosis.

cutoff_values.value: Urate-lowering treat-to-target: serum urate <360 micromol/L (6 mg/dL), or <300 micromol/L for tophaceous/severe disease (EULAR/ACR).

differential_diagnosis.differences: Systemically unwell/fever, cannot be excluded clinically - MUST aspirate
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have a fever or feel systemically unwell?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Often knee/wrist, older, positively birefringent rhomboid crystals, chondrocalcinosis
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it a larger joint like the knee/wrist in an older person?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Skin infection pattern, spreading erythema, portal of entry, less joint-centred
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Diffuse skin erythema, less joint-line tenderness
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the redness in the skin rather than centred on the joint?
Any recent infection or other joint/eye/skin symptoms?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a fever or feel systemically unwell with this hot joint?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Fever/systemic illness -> aspirate urgently to exclude sepsis

diagnostic_questions.question: Did it come on within hours in the big toe, and have you had similar attacks before?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Rapid podagra + prior attacks -> gout likely

next_best_question.question: Any fever/systemic illness, and is this a typical rapid big-toe attack with prior episodes?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Systemically unwell/uncertain -> urgent aspiration to exclude septic arthritis; typical gout -> treat the attack + plan urate-lowering

next_best_test.test: Joint aspiration (if infection possible or diagnosis uncertain)
next_best_test.why: Confirms crystals and excludes septic arthritis

red_flags.finding: Hot, swollen joint with fever or systemic illness
red_flags.immediate_action: Treat as possible septic arthritis - urgent aspiration/orthopaedic referral before assuming gout

red_flags.finding: Multiple joints, immunosuppression, or prosthetic joint involved
Rapidly progressive joint destruction or systemic sepsis
Severe tophaceous disease with renal impairment
red_flags.immediate_action: Specialist rheumatology input for urate lowering

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected septic arthritis (emergency); diagnostic uncertainty needing aspiration.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Refractory/frequent attacks, tophaceous gout, urate-lowering difficulties (CKD, intolerance), or uncertain diagnosis.

late: Chronic tophaceous gout with joint damage

initial_management.supportive_care: Rest and elevate the joint; ice; explain the condition and the plan for prevention.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): NSAID; Colchicine; Corticosteroid; Allopurinol or other urate-lowering therapy. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG219.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Reduce alcohol (especially beer) and sugary/fructose drinks, moderate purine-rich foods, weight loss, hydration; review diuretics; manage cardiovascular/renal risk.
initial_management.follow_up: Titrate urate-lowering therapy to target serum urate; monitor renal function and attack frequency.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Acute attack: NSAID (with gastroprotection) OR colchicine OR corticosteroid (oral/intra-articular), chosen by comorbidity/renal function - start early. Long-term: offer urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol first-line; febuxostat alternative) treat-to-target, especially with recurrent attacks, tophi, renal stones, or CKD; start after an attack settles with prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine or NSAID) during initiation; do NOT stop urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack if already established.

patient_education.home_advice: Gout is caused by uric acid crystals in the joint, giving sudden very painful, red, swollen attacks (often the big toe). Treat attacks early with the medicine your doctor advises. To prevent attacks long-term, a daily tablet (like allopurinol) lowers uric acid - keep taking it every day, even between attacks. Cut down alcohol and sugary drinks, lose excess weight, and drink water. Seek urgent care if a hot joint comes with fever, as that could be a joint infection.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: النقرس سببه بلورات حمض اليوريك في المفصل، فتحدث نوبات مفاجئة شديدة الألم مع احمرار وتورّم (غالباً إبهام القدم). عالِج النوبات مبكراً بالدواء الذي يصفه طبيبك. وللوقاية طويلة الأمد، حبة يومية (مثل الألوبيورينول) تخفض حمض اليوريك - استمرّ عليها يومياً حتى بين النوبات. قلّل الكحول والمشروبات السكرية، وأنقِص الوزن الزائد، واشرب الماء. اطلب الرعاية العاجلة إذا صاحب المفصل الحار حرارةٌ، فقد يكون عدوى في المفصل.
patient_education.prevention: Weight management, limit alcohol/sugary drinks, hydration, urate-lowering therapy to target.
patient_education.warning_signs: Hot joint with fever/feeling unwell (possible infection), or frequent recurrent attacks.

prevention.lifestyle: Diet, alcohol reduction, weight loss, hydration; review urate-raising drugs.

evidence.evidence_level: High for acute treatments and treat-to-target urate lowering.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG219; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong - NICE NG219, EULAR, ACR, BSR.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Treat flares promptly and reduce recurrent crystal burden using treat-to-target urate lowering.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): NSAID; Colchicine; Corticosteroid; Allopurinol or other urate-lowering therapy. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG219.

pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances

non_drug_measures: Hydration, healthy weight and review of alcohol/diet and urate-raising medicines without blaming the patient.

monitoring: renal function, blood pressure, oedema and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms when clinically indicated
